name: Ouidah: Route of Slaves and Door of No Return
subtitle: Ouidah is a town on the Beninese coast, about forty kilometres from Cotonou, that was the port of the Hueda Kingdom and a major embarkation point of the Atlantic slave trade.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: Coastal town about 40 km from Cotonou

facts.label: Earlier name and kingdom
facts.value: Called Gléwé, port of the Hueda Kingdom, when Europeans arrived in the late 15th century

facts.label: Departures
facts.value: About 10,000 enslaved people left Ouidah each year by the end of the 17th century

facts.label: Door of No Return
facts.value: Monument at the end of a two-mile dirt road, described as commemorating some one million enslaved people

facts.label: Inaugurated
facts.value: 30 November 1995, by the Government of Benin and UNESCO

facts.label: Start of the route
facts.value: Place des enchères (place Chacha), town centre

facts.label: Mortality at sea
facts.value: On average 20% of those embarked died during the crossing

facts.label: Museum of History
facts.value: Housed in a Portuguese fort built in 1721

parts.text: Ouidah is a town on the Beninese coast, about forty kilometres from Cotonou, that was the port of the Hueda Kingdom and a major embarkation point of the Atlantic slave trade. The Door of No Return, a monument inaugurated in 1995 on the beach, marks the end of the route that captives walked from the town's auction square. Archaeology Magazine describes it as a monument to some one million enslaved people.
